title_en: How to Apologise Like a Briton
description_ru: Шутливое руководство для иностранцев по британским извинениям, вежливым отказам и тому, что на самом деле значит «мне очень жаль».
text:
If you spend a week in Britain, you will hear the word "sorry" about four hundred times. It will be said by people who have stepped on your foot, by people whose foot you have stepped on, by people who are merely standing in the same room as a foot, and, on one occasion that I personally witnessed, by a man who walked into a lamp post. This is not because the British are an unusually guilty nation. It is because "sorry" is not an apology at all. It is a kind of verbal Swiss army knife, and learning to use it is the key to survival.

Let us begin with the basic model. When a Briton says "sorry" in the street, it usually means "excuse me". When he says it in a shop, it often means "please move". When he says it on the telephone, it can mean "I did not hear you", "I disagree" or "I am about to complain about something, so please brace yourself". The only situation in which it generally does not mean "I regret what I have done" is when someone has actually done something wrong. In that case, the preferred expression is "Oh dear".

Visitors are often bewildered by what is known as the polite refusal. Suppose you are invited to a dinner party and asked whether you would like a second helping. If the host says, "Would you like a bit more?", the correct reply is "Oh, I couldn't possibly". This does not mean no. It means "Please ask me again, and then I shall accept, with a show of reluctance". If you say yes immediately, you will be considered greedy. If you say no and mean it, you will go hungry, and nobody will ever realise what has happened.

There is also a rich vocabulary of understatement, and it is important to know how to translate it. When a British person says "That's quite good", he usually means that it is excellent, unless he is from the south, in which case he probably means that it is mediocre. When he says "I was a bit worried", he has just survived a catastrophe. "It's not ideal" means the building is on fire. And "With the greatest respect" is always followed by a remark that is not respectful in the least. Foreign business people have been known to leave meetings completely convinced that they had been praised, only to discover that they had been fired.

The queue, of course, is sacred. In Britain, nobody will ever tell you that you have pushed in. Instead, there will be a silence, a cough, and a sudden, extraordinary tension in the air, as if a mild earthquake had occurred. Seven people will glance at one another. One of them might murmur, "Sorry, I think the end is over there", in a tone that says you have just insulted the monarch. The correct reply is to apologise profusely, to blush and to move to the back, where you will be silently forgiven. Then, you will be expected to complain about the weather.

The weather deserves its own paragraph. The British discuss it constantly, but never in the way you might think. When a stranger on a train says, "Nice day, isn't it?", he is not really interested in meteorology. He is saying, "I come in peace". The right answer is "Lovely", even if it is pouring with rain, because the conversation can then continue safely to the topic of how it was much better last week. It is a form of friendship that requires no personal information whatsoever, which is precisely why it works.

Another important phrase is "I'll let you get on". This means that the speaker has been trying to end a telephone call for twenty minutes. A related expression, "We must do lunch", is an invitation that is never intended to be taken up, and it is considered rude to look for a diary. "Pop round any time" means "please telephone first". And "Do come in, don't mind the mess" means that the house has been cleaned for three days and that you must say it looks wonderful.

Of course, this is a generalisation, and many Britons are perfectly direct. I have met some who say exactly what they mean, and they are generally regarded with a mixture of awe and alarm. But if you stay long enough, you will discover that this elaborate system of hints is not hypocrisy at all. It is a way of being kind. Everybody understands the code, and nobody is ever humiliated. Disagreement is wrapped up like a present, in so many layers of paper that it is almost impossible to find what is inside.

So, if you are planning to visit, practise the following. Apologise to doors. Thank the bus driver, even if he has not stopped. Say "Cheers" when you leave a shop, "Lovely" when you do not mean it, and "Sorry" at any moment when you cannot think of anything else. If somebody apologises to you, apologise back, and continue until one of you leaves the room. I am terribly sorry that this essay was so long. I do hope you didn't mind.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Губы округлены вперёд, без касания зубами; не путайте с «в».
Тот же положение языка, что для θ, но с голосом: звук гудит, не «з».
Ударение ставьте на нужный слог: ударный слог длиннее, громче и выше по тону, остальные сокращаются.
Задняя часть языка к мягкому нёбу, звук идёт через нос; не добавляйте «г» в конце.

questions.question: What does the word sorry usually mean in Britain?
questions.answer: Often it means excuse me, not a real apology.

questions.question: What should you answer if offered a second helping?
questions.answer: Say you couldn't possibly, and wait to be asked again.

questions.question: What does a stranger mean by saying nice day?
questions.answer: He is being friendly: I come in peace.

questions.question: What does I'll let you get on mean?
questions.answer: The speaker wants to end the phone call.
